D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b000_.text: Honey, see this jar of soapy water? My mother kept one just like it on the windowsill over the farm sink, and I still do. We were poor. We just didn't know it because of these little tricks. Nobody on our farm called the exterminator. Pull up that chair and sit with me. I'm 81 years old, and I've got all afternoon. Last time, honey, we talked about the mice that start moving in when the nights turn cold and the five spots to seal before the first frost. If you missed it, it's the video called Mice Are Moving In Right Now. Today is about everything else she did to keep the house shut up tight the whole year round. Here is what we're going to do. 15 tricks numbered one to 15, and every one came out of my mother's kitchen. I'll tell you what each one costs, what it works on, and how long it takes.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b001_.text: and I'll tell you honestly which ones don't work by themselves because the internet is full of tricks that only move the bugs into the next room. Each one has a page in my little book and I'll tell you where. Some of these you'll already do and some will surprise you. Either way, you'll finish with a dry sink and a tight pantry. Before you spend a single dollar, let me tell you what doesn't work. Plug -in sound repellers don't keep mice away for long. Sealing the hole does. Dryer sheets in the drawers mask a smell for about a week. They don't keep mice out. I'll get to what does work and what it costs in just a minute. Bug bombs just scatter the roaches deeper into the walls where you can't reach them. I grew up on a farm in Story County, Iowa. We lived next to a barn, a chicken house and a corn crib and every bug and mouse in the county wanted into my mother's kitchen.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b002_.text: Almost none of them got in. She didn't have a spray for every bug. She had three ideas, and they're the whole book. Close the door, take away the food, make them want to leave. Poison was the last resort because there were children underfoot and a dog and a cat. We didn't have much money. My mother kept that house with pennies and a dish towel. She didn't call it a plan. She called it Keeping House. I never once thought we were poor. Every trick I'm going to tell you about today is written out in my little book with the steps, the exact costs, and where each one works. Trick number one is on page nine and the link is down in the description, right under this video. Now honey, let's get started. Trick number one is the dime walk. You can't keep out what you haven't found and mice come in through gaps nobody looks at.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b003_.text: My mother walked the outside of the house at ground level with a flashlight. She checked where the pipes, the wires, the gas line, and the dryer vent go into the wall. Anywhere a dime fits, she stuffed it tight with steel wool, then sealed it with caulk so the wool stays put. Here is Loretta's trick. Mice chew right through foam and caulk alone, but they won't chew through steel wool. That's why it's both. Wear gloves for the steel wool and don't block the furnace or dryer vents because those get metal mesh covers. It costs about eight to $15 and takes one afternoon. It's on page nine of my little book. Trick number two is under the sinks. The hole where the pipes go through the wall under the kitchen sink is the front door for mice. Empty that cabinet, all of it, and look at where the pipes go into the wall. That hole is almost always bigger than the pipe.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b004_.text: Pack steel wool around the pipe, then caulk over it. Do the bathroom sinks the same way. The mistake most people make is missing the back corner. So shine the flashlight in from below and look at it the way a mouse would. It costs about $3 and takes 20 minutes. Nothing about this is dangerous for children or pets. It's on page 10. Trick number three is the door sweep. Daylight under an outside door is a mouse door, honey. Plain as day. Measure the door's width and cut the sweep to length. Hold it on the inside bottom of the door so the brush just touches the floor and screw it on. Here is Loretta's trick. The garage door has a rubber strip on the bottom too and if it's cracked, that's where they get in. A good sweep keeps out mice, the cold air, and a good many bugs. It costs about $8 to $15 and takes 20 minutes. It's on page 11 of my little book.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b005_.text: Trick number four is nothing to eat. A mouse that finds food stays, honey, and a mouse that finds nothing moves on. My mother moved every bag of flour, sugar, rice, oats, crackers, pet food, and bird seed out of its paper bag and into a glass jar, a metal tin, or a hard plastic bin with a tight lid. Here is Loretta's trick. Bird seed and dog food sitting in the garage are the number one reason mice move in for the winter. Food and paper, or thin plastic, gets chewed through in one night. The jars cost about five to $20 in all, and it takes about an hour. It's on page 12. Trick number five is peppermint, and I'll be honest about it. Peppermint oil is everywhere on the internet. You can put a few drops on cotton balls and small jar lids behind the stove, under the sink, and in the pantry. Refresh them every three or four days because the smell fades fast.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b006_.text: The mistake is using peppermint instead of sealing the holes, because a smell doesn't close a door. Think of it as making this room unpleasant, not as making them leave the house. And peppermint oil is harmful to cats and can bother dogs, so keep it out of reach or skip it. It costs about $5 to $8 a bottle and takes 5 minutes. It's on page 13. Trick number 6 is a dry kitchen at night. Roaches can live about a month without food, honey, but only about a week without water. So my mother's rule was a dry sink at bedtime. Dish is done, nothing soaking overnight, and the dish rag hung up instead of left in a wet heap. Fix any dripping faucet or leaking pipe under the sink. Here is Loretta's trick. The mistake is the pet water bowl left on the kitchen floor overnight. That's a water stop for the roaches. This costs nothing and takes 5 minutes a night.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b007_.text: It's on page 23 of my little book. Trick number seven is the boxes and bags from the store. Roaches and their eggs ride into the house on cardboard boxes and paper grocery bags, and nobody thinks about it. So unpack on the porch or in the garage. Break down the boxes and take them straight out to the bin, and never store paper bags under the sink, honey. A stack of them behind the refrigerator is a roach apartment building. Here is Loretta's trick. Saving the boxes in the kitchen gives the bugs a hiding place, so don't. It costs nothing, and it takes two minutes every trip from the store. Nothing about it is dangerous. It's on page 24 of my little book. Trick number eight is the trail, and that's where the jar of soapy water comes in, the one you saw at the very start. Ants keep coming back because they follow a scent trail.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b008_.text: So you follow it backward, away from the food, to the place where they come in. A window corner, a crack, a pipe. Once the bait has done its job, you wipe the trail with the soapy water because ants follow a scent line, then caulk the crack they came through. If you use bait at all, keep it where children and pets can't reach it, because borax is harmful if swallowed. The bait and its safety rules are on page 18 of my little book, and please read them first. The mistake is wiping the trail before the bait has done its work, so the ants scatter everywhere. This costs pennies and takes about 20 minutes. The trail itself is on page 19. This is why I wrote it all down, honey. Every one of these tricks has its own page, so you never have to hunt for the page. If you're watching this on the television, grab your phone and look up my little book.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b009_.text: Once the ants are gone, let's talk about the next thing that wants into your kitchen. Trick number nine is the chalk and cinnamon line. Ants coming in at one doorway or one window sill. Draw a thick line of plain sidewalk chalk across the sill or the threshold or sprinkle ground cinnamon along it. It breaks up their scent path and that buys you a little time. Here is Loretta's trick. It's a fence, not a cure, honey. The mistake is using only this because then they'll simply find the next crack over. So keep the line up while the bait works and redo it after you clean or after a good ring. It costs pennies and takes two minutes. It's on page 22 of my little book. Trick number 10 is peroxide on contact. A roach on the counter or a line of ants across the bread and you don't want poison anywhere near the food.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b010_.text: So grab the brown bottle of 3 % hydrogen peroxide with the spray nozzle. Spray the roach or the ants until they're wet and wipe them up with a paper towel. Here is Loretta's trick, it's safe on the counter. The mistake is thinking it fixes the whole problem when it only gets the ones in front of you. Peroxide can lighten fabric in dark wood and it does not kill or drive out mice. A bottle costs about a dollar and it's on page 21. Trick number 11 is for the pantry moths. Little moths around the kitchen and webby clumps in the flour. Empty the whole pantry, throw out anything with webs, worms or clumps and vacuum the shelves and the holes the shelf pegs sit in. Then comes the part my mother never skipped. She froze every new bag of flour, oats, rice and birdseed for four days before it went into a jar. Then everything went into sealed jars.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b011_.text: Here is Loretta's trick. Bay leaves in the jars and on the shelves. The mistake is keeping just the good part of a bag because the eggs are invisible, honey. Throw out the whole bag. This costs between nothing and about $15 and it takes one afternoon. It's on page 30 of my little book. Trick number 12 is the wool. Holes in the sweaters you put away clean in the spring come from moths. Wash or dry clean the wool before you put it away because the moths go for the sweat and the food spots. Store it in zippered bags and put cedar blocks or lavender sachets in with it. Here is Loretta's trick. Sand the cedar blocks lightly each spring and they smell new again. The mistake is putting the sweaters away after wearing them only once because that's what the moths eat. And no mothballs in the house, honey. They're a poison you breathe.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b012_.text: The cedar or lavender costs about $5 to $15. It's on page 31. Trick number 13 is no standing water. Mosquitoes can breed in a bottle cap of water in a single week. So every week, tip out the flower pot saucers, the buckets, the toys, and the old tarps. Clean the gutters so they don't hold water and keep the rain barrel covered with screen. The worst one, my mother said, was the saucer under the porch planter. Fill it with sand and it can't hold water at all. Here is Loretta's trick. The mistake most people make is forgetting the gutters. Nothing about this costs a thing and it takes about 15 minutes a week. It's on page 35. Trick number 14 is wood and mulch away from the house. Firewood and mulch piled against the foundation are a highway for ants, roaches, and termites.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b013_.text: So pull the mulch back 12 inches, leaving a strip of bare soil or gravel. Stack the firewood at least 20 feet from the house and up off the ground. Trim the bushes so they don't touch the walls or the roof and bring in only the firewood you'll burn that same day. Here is Loretta's trick. A wood pile on the porch is a winter home for mice. The mistake is keeping a wood pile on the porch. And honey, if you see mud tubes on the foundation or the wood sounds hollow when you knock on it, call a termite inspector. Don't try that one yourself. It's on page 36. Trick number 15 is the slugs. Lacy holes in the lettuce and silver trails across the path in the morning. Lay a board on the soil in the evening and in the morning lift it up and remove the slugs hiding underneath.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b014_.text: Sink a shallow dish into the soil, up to the rim, and fill it with a little cheap beer, and they crawl right in. Water the garden in the morning, not the evening, because slugs love damp nights. Here is Loretta's trick. Never use salt on slugs in the garden, because it ruins the soil. Keep the beer dish where the pets can't drink from it, honey. It costs pennies and takes about 10 minutes. It's on page 38 of my little book. So here are the 15. One more time. Seal the holes, the doors and the pipes. Take away the food and put it in jars. Keep the sink dry and the boxes out of the house. Keep the water out of the saucers and the mulch away from the walls. My little book says the whole kit comes to about $60, and that's less than one visit from an exterminator, honey, with his truck and his tank.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b015_.text: Borax, boric acid, and peppermint oil are not safe for children or for pets, so they go up high, behind a closed cabinet, or they don't go in the house at all. And if you have a real infestation, termites, bed bugs, or mice you hear in the walls every night, the book says plainly to call a professional, and I say the same. Page 46 has the list. Don't be too proud to call. Those are the honest words for today. The few things I do buy, with what each one costs, are on page 45 of my little book. The link to my little book is right under this video in the description. Now I have a question for you, and I do want you to answer it in the comments. Which one of these 15 does your kitchen need first, honey? Tell me what's been getting into your house this year. In the next video, when you're ready, is how my mother kept every fly out of a farm kitchen.

D:\\wt\\fhpoor\\vlog\\fhpoor\\voz\\b016_.text: It starts with a lemon with cloves pushed into it, sitting right there on the sill. Over on my church kitchen channel, there's a video called Most People Make Mashed Potatoes Wrong. Try these church lady tricks before Thanksgiving. That's all my mother knew, honey, and nothing got past her. Close the door, take away the food, and make them want to leave. It'll work for your house too. May the Lord keep your pantry dry and your doors shut tight. God bless you, and I'll see you next time.
